items.title: The Reluctant Winner of the AI Race
items.description: Over the past few weeks, the AI industry has teetered closer to financial calamity than ever. Investors have begun asking more questions about tremendous and circular spending that is funding the AI build-out. Major AI data-center players are loading up on more and more debt, some of it in the form of junk bonds. In the midterm elections, Americans overwhelmingly voted for referendums and candidates that would slow data-center development. And then, as if that weren’t enough uncertainty, Jensen Huang admitted last week to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and stepped down as CEO of Nvidia—the AI-chipmaking giant that has been the financial backstop for the AI boom. Even before the uncertainty produced by Huang’s resignation, Nvidia was reportedly considering curbing some of its spending commitments. In other words, if this is a bubble, about now would be the time for it to pop. [ Read: ] A $5.7 Trillion Face-Plant And yet, tomorrow, amid this tremendous uncertainty, Anthropic will forge ahead with its immense public offering—beginning to trade on stock exchanges and aiming to raise more than $90 billion in the process, which would be the most of any IPO ever. The timing could either be calamitous or turn out to be a coup. Demand is red-hot: The company reportedly received nearly seven times more orders than there are shares available. Anthropic may emerge not just as one of the world’s largest companies but as the AI trade’s latest savior and lynchpin. That’s not, however, necessarily good news for the rest of our economic well-being. Tomorrow’s public offering will cap off an astounding 12 months for the company. For years, Anthropic was known as OpenAI’s safety-forward younger sibling. Formed by Dario Amodei and six other former OpenAI employees in 2021, the company consistently operated in the shadow of its older sibling, which became the face of the AI industry. That changed last November, when Anthropic released a new model, Claude Opus 4.5. The model was widely considered to represent a step change in AI capabilities, helped usher in the era of agentic AI, and pushed Anthropic to the front of the pack. Many of the company’s core, early bets—its emphasis on AI coding and other workplace tools, its positioning as being safety- and responsibility-first—paid off. While OpenAI focused on consumer products such as a chatbot and a TikTok-style AI-video app, Anthropic attracted big enterprise customers. Anthropic’s quarterly revenues, according to its IPO filings, have grown more than eightfold since the end of 2025. Just from July to September of this year, the company made more than $16 billion. If, even a year ago, you’d told any analyst that Anthropic would go public before OpenAI, they’d be shocked. Now it seems obvious. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.) If Anthropic’s public offering goes well, it will fuel renewed confidence and investment in the industry as a whole and, perhaps, fix its wobble. Anthropic’s listing on stock markets (“ANT,” if you’re curious) can be taken as a sign of maturation—evidence that Anthropic and AI, as a major force in the economy, are here to stay. Not only is the company’s revenue growth meteoric; it expects its spending—money that will flow throughout the data-center and AI ecosystem—to grow in lockstep. Anthropic is committed to spending more than $900 billion on data centers and related infrastructure, and said in its IPO paperwork that it expects its expenditures to only “increase significantly.” Being bullish on Anthropic means, by necessity, being bullish on AI; it means believing that, at some point, all of this spending pays off, yielding, as Anthropic states in its founders’ letter, cures for cancer and Alzheimer’s disease, alongside tens of trillions of dollars in global economic growth. Any number of investors looking to sell shares of Nvidia could switch that money over to Anthropic, and Amodei could assume the role of Jensen Huang: the steadfast and responsible shepherd of the industry. Of course, the opposite could happen. Should Anthropic’s offering flop, it will almost certainly kick off an extended period of pain for Silicon Valley. Anthropic’s demand for more and more computing power—to train more powerful models and serve more customers—is perhaps the single most important indicator of the strength of the data-center boom. If investors prove nervous about even this company, which is cleanly winning the AI-capabilities race and growing its revenues at a historic pace, then the entire edifice is suspect. And a successful IPO, in and of itself, would reflect good vibes but not directly change the underlying mismatch between revenues and planned spending across the AI industry, Anthropic included. Another $900 billion in promised AI and data-center expenditures may not make this infrastructure boom more sustainable—but it could add to losses if and when the bubble does pop. Perhaps the most likely course is somewhere in between total AI dominance and collapse. Anthropic goes public and sees sustained, even spectacular, success as a business and a stock. The AI-investment flywheel , flush with new cash, spins ever faster. Fortune 500 companies that deploy Claude agents see their profit margins rise. Meanwhile: All of the AI money flooding markets, alongside spending on data-center construction, keeps inflation high. All of those agents mean that the labor force remains stagnant, or shrinks. If you listen to Anthropic’s communications, both the IPO and the company’s immediate profits are secondary concerns. The company’s prospectus warns investors, again and again, that it might make decisions that do not maximize profits. And that significant increase in spending, Anthropic notes, “may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves.” That cavalier attitude toward making money is in line with Anthropic’s origins as a safety-oriented AI lab (and it was, at the start, genuinely a lab). It’s also in line with Anthropic leadership’s zealotry about the inevitability and imminence of superintelligence, which stands out even among their AI-executive peers. Going public, and all of the capital that allows Anthropic to access, is a sign that the firm is intent in securing its role in dictating the direction of such all-powerful machines. This IPO lands at a time of anxiety about AI as the technology of the future. Rogue-agent swarms and a deluge of AI-powered cyberattacks have left many wondering whether the industry should slow down and led many to suggest that it do so—including Amodei himself . And yet, Anthropic is forging ahead, shutting down fear and criticism just as all of its peers have done at every turn; the AI industry’s self-styled superego may turn out to be the id. Anthropic was founded, above all, on faith in Amodei’s clairvoyance and judgment. Seemingly the Anthropic CEO’s most candid answer to why he’d left OpenAI was in a Bloomberg interview this past summer in which he said, “Why argue with someone when you don’t have the same vision and you don’t trust them? The way to resolve it is: You go off and do your thing; they go off and do their thing.” Going public is entirely consistent with such messianism. What sets Anthropic apart is that it is a company of true believers—in the almost transcendental power of AI and, as important, in themselves. Last year, at Anthropic’s headquarters, I had a telling conversation with two of its researchers, Trenton Bricken and Sholto Douglas. Bricken was telling me that in an ideal world, he’d want AI development to proceed far more slowly and carefully. Douglas disagreed: Any delay “comes at the cost of millions of lives,” he told me. At the time, I wrote that the impulses to speed and slow AI development seemed to be at war within the company. Now one side has clearly won out.

items.title: Ghana’s unemployed youth seek jobs, but say their voices remain absent from decision-making
items.description: With unemployment remaining one of the biggest concerns confronting young people in Ghana, three youth leaders are calling for greater involvement of the younger generation in decisions on governance, public policy and national development. They argue that young people must not only be recognised as the country’s future leaders but also given meaningful opportunities to influence decisions on issues that directly affect their lives, particularly employment, education and economic opportunities. Their concerns feature in “We Shall Lead: Voices Shaping the Future of Africa,” a documentary that examines the participation of young people and women in politics and public life, highlighting the barriers that prevent them from assuming leadership roles and influencing public decisions. The documentary features three Ghanaian youth leaders: Hariratah Ibrahim Doudu, Vice President of the Student Representative Council (SRC) of the Ghana School of Law; Rashid Ibrahim, President of the National Union of Ghana Students (NUGS); and Sherif Ghali, Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Chamber of Young Entrepreneurs and President of the Ghana Youth Federation. Their experiences point to a wider concern: while young people are expected to contribute to national development, their concerns and perspectives are not always adequately reflected in the institutions and processes responsible for shaping the country’s future. Unemployment deepens the call for youth inclusion The concerns are supported by labour market figures from the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), which show that unemployment remains significantly higher among young people than the national average. The GSS Quarterly Labour Force Survey for the first three quarters of 2025 put national unemployment at an average of 12.8 per cent, compared with 21.9 per cent among people aged 15 to 35 and 32.4 per cent among those aged 15 to 24. The figures also showed that nearly two million people aged 15 to 35, representing about 19.5 per cent of that age group, were neither in employment nor education or training by the third quarter of 2025. A 2025 Afrobarometer study on Ghanaian youth also found that about 34 per cent of young people aged 18 to 35 were looking for work, despite three-quarters having secondary or post-secondary qualifications. The study further found that 72 per cent of young Ghanaians had considered emigrating, with many citing the search for employment and better economic opportunities. The figures highlight the need for young people to be involved in shaping employment policies and other national interventions, rather than remaining recipients of decisions made without sufficient consideration of their experiences. The concern also has implications for national stability. In May 2026, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) warned that youth disillusionment and unemployment could threaten Ghana’s peace and security through social unrest, radicalisation and conflict. UNDP Resident Representative in Ghana, Mr Niloy Banerjee, stressed the importance of keeping young people productively engaged to protect the country’s stability. Young people want influence beyond representation For Mr Ibrahim, the decision to seek student leadership was motivated by the need to create a platform where young people could raise concerns and have their views considered by those in authority. He said young people had the knowledge, energy and capacity to contribute to national development but needed opportunities to demonstrate their abilities and participate in decision-making. “The youthful leaders are doing well. Why don’t we give them the opportunity,” he asked, arguing that young people could make meaningful contributions if given the right platforms and support. Mr Ghali said the challenge went beyond appointing young people to leadership positions, stressing that genuine inclusion required giving them the authority to influence decisions. “The struggle is so serious that young people do not want to go into politics. It is not about including us but allowing us to take decisions,” he said. He said young people would develop greater confidence in democratic institutions when they saw their concerns reflected in public policies and their peers actively involved in shaping national priorities. Ms Doudu also highlighted institutional barriers that could discourage young people, particularly women, from seeking leadership positions. “The system of politics is not really created to accommodate women. It is now, in these days, that the system is trying to accommodate women,” she said. Drawing on her experience at the Ghana School of Law, she recalled that no woman had attempted to contest the SRC vice-presidency for more than five years before she decided to run, despite women outnumbering men at the institution. She said her personal circumstances, including losing her father after senior high school, had strengthened her determination to lead and encourage others to challenge existing barriers. Representation must translate into participation The concerns raised by the three leaders reflect wider questions about youth representation in Ghana’s democratic institutions. Young people aged 15 to 35 constitute about 38.2 per cent of Ghana’s population, according to the 2021 Population and Housing Census, yet their representation in national decision-making remains limited. Data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union at the beginning of the current Parliament in January 2025 recorded 46 Members of Parliament aged 40 or younger, out of 276 legislators. Afrobarometer’s 2025 research on political participation also found that young Africans were generally less involved than older generations in several civic and political activities, including voting, attending community meetings and contacting elected representatives. Its findings showed an 18-percentage-point gap between younger and older citizens in voter participation. The documentary is part of the European Union-funded Women and Youth Democratic Engagement (WYDE) Political Parties Project, led by the European Network of Political Foundations (ENoP) and implemented in Ghana by the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung (KAS) Ghana Office. The project seeks to strengthen the participation of young people and women in democratic processes through leadership training, mentorship and capacity-building workshops. It also features experiences from political and public leaders in Kenya and Uganda, with the aim of extending lessons on inclusive leadership beyond the project’s direct beneficiaries. The documentary ultimately raises a central question for Ghana’s democracy: how can the country address the pressing concerns of its young population when those most affected have limited influence over the decisions intended to shape their future? items.title: Tunisia olive oil exports jump nearly 50 pct on bumper harvest
items.description: Tunisia's olive oil exports rose nearly 50 percent, official figures showed on Wednesday, after a bumper harvest that made it the world's second biggest producer after Spain. Exports jumped 47.7 percent to 413,100 tonnes during the season that ended in October, earning revenues of $1.7 billion, the National Agricultural Observatory said. Tunisia produced more than 500,000 tonnes of olive oil this season, a five-year record. Agriculture accounts for 10 percent of the country's GDP, according to official figures.

items.title: IET-GH donates medical equipment to Osu Maternity Clinic
items.description: The Institution of Engineering and Technology Ghana (IET-GH) has donated medical equipment and cash to the Osu Maternity Clinic to support healthcare delivery at the facility. The donation forms part of activities marking the institution’s 40th Annual General Meeting (AGM) and Engineering Conference and also reflects its commitment to giving back to society and supporting communities in need. The items presented included patient screens, four 20-litre oxygen cylinders, three oxygen flow meters and a suction machine, together with an undisclosed amount of money. Speaking during the presentation, the President of IET-GH, Engr. Wonder Davor, said the donation was informed by the institution’s belief that its responsibility extended beyond promoting professional engineering practice to addressing the needs of society. He said the gesture was inspired by Matthew 25:35, which emphasises the importance of helping people in need. “As an engineering institution, we believe that we should not only focus on professional engineering practice but also extend a helping hand to people who need support,” he said. Engr. Davor expressed hope that the equipment would help improve healthcare delivery at the facility and contribute to saving lives. He explained that the items were selected after consultations with the clinic’s authorities to identify equipment that was urgently needed. According to him, the institution decided to support the facility as part of its activities marking the 40th anniversary celebrations and its annual professional gathering. He also outlined the programme for the two-day event, announcing that the Engineering Conference would take place on November 19 at the Shippers Council. The conference is expected to provide a platform for discussions on key professional issues, while also recognising and honouring individuals who have made outstanding contributions to the engineering profession. The AGM, scheduled for November 20, will focus on the institution’s financial accounts, accountability to members and plans for its future development. Receiving the donation on behalf of the facility, Senior Administrative Manager of the Osu Maternity Clinic, Aminatu Sharif, said that the support was timely and significant, given the clinic’s role in providing healthcare services to residents of Osu and surrounding communities. She explained that the facility, which traditionally provided maternity services, had expanded its operations to include general outpatient care following the addition of a medical doctor and a physician assistant. “It used to be a maternity home where we only took care of pregnant women. However, we now have a doctor and a physician assistant who attend to general outpatient cases,” she said. She noted that the expansion had transformed the clinic into a facility providing a wider range of healthcare services, increasing the need for equipment, infrastructure and other essential resources. Madam Sharif said the clinic was one of the major government healthcare facilities serving the Osu community, making support from individuals, corporate institutions and other stakeholders important to its operations. She appealed to organisations and the public to support the facility, stressing that government alone could not address all its infrastructure and operational challenges. “We need all the help that people can give us. We are serving the people and delivering healthcare services, but we need a lot of improvement, which the government alone cannot provide,” she said. Among the major challenges facing the facility, she identified inadequate space and structural limitations, which she said prevented the clinic from introducing additional services that could improve healthcare delivery. She explained that upgrading the existing structure, potentially into a multi-storey building, would create more space for additional departments and enable the clinic to offer a wider range of services. Madam Sharif also identified the need for everyday consumables, office equipment and medical machines as some of the facility’s pressing requirements. She said addressing these challenges would improve the clinic’s capacity to provide quality healthcare to the growing number of people who depend on its services. She also expressed appreciation to IET-GH for the donation and assured the institution that the items and financial support would be used for their intended purposes.

items.title: How Jared Kushner Sparked a Revolution in the Balkans
items.description: O n the eighth day of violent protests in Tirana, I followed a column of some 3,000 people marching through the Albanian capital. For months, Albanians had held anti-government demonstrations as peaceful as the pink bird that had lent their movement its name—the Flamingo Revolution. But the protests had recently entered a new, volatile phase. Some had begun calling it the Eagle Revolution, after the fiercer bird on the national flag. It was 1 p.m. on a Tuesday in October, and demonstrators filled the downtown boulevards. We walked past shattered bus shelters, broken shop windows, and government buildings blackened by fire. “Down with the patronazhistët ,” people shouted, referring to the entrenched patronage networks that reward party loyalty over merit in nearly every sphere of life. When another group chanted a World War II slogan—“Albania for the Albanians, death to the traitors”—my fixer said, “This one is for you.” He meant Americans. What had first sparked the protests, in May, were plans by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of the American president, to build an ultra-luxury resort in a fragile nature preserve in the country’s south, where flamingos gather. The marchers stopped outside the education ministry. I moved to the front, where the most aggressive protesters were. The “fire team,” some called them: lanky youths in masks and reflective ski goggles. Several of them wrenched paving stones from the sidewalk, smashed them against the curb, and launched the pieces at the ministry’s windows by hand and slingshot. State police officers, leaning on riot shields, watched impassively for about 15 minutes. Then a heavy police truck with rooftop water cannons maneuvered onto the street. My fixer pushed me through the crowd as jets of water raked our backs. That evening, after dark, the streets outside the prime minister’s office boomed with small explosions. Police in riot gear rolled through with tear-gas launchers. Protesters tossed Molotov cocktails that broke in flames at officers’ feet. Albania is one of Europe’s poorest countries. From a nation of 2.3 million, some 40,000 citizens leave each year. The list of prominent politicians recently charged with corruption—by a special prosecutor’s office, created under pressure from the European Union and the United States—includes a former prime minister, a deputy prime minister, a former president, and the mayor of Tirana, who presides from his jail cell. A Miami businessman who sold Kushner and his partners land for the resort is being investigated by Albanian prosecutors for allegedly forging the deeds and laundering money for drug gangs. (All of them maintain their innocence. Kushner has not been accused of wrongdoing.) I wanted to speak with college students at the forefront of these new protests—young people so furious about government corruption that they’d spent months in the streets. Almost nothing like it has occurred in our own country, despite nearly 90 percent of Americans—a 20-year high, according to Gallup— seeing corruption as widespread . In an October CNBC survey , voters ranked corruption as their top issue, ahead of food costs. But for many Americans, the issue seems remote—a problem that troubles them intellectually yet doesn’t touch their lives in the intimate ways that it does Albanians’. Prime Minister Edi Rama and his center-left Socialist Party have held power for 13 years. Party leaders, protesters told me, influence who gets jobs, contracts, and government services. Graft abounds. In a 2025 survey, nearly 10 percent of public-university students admitted that they’d offered bribes for better grades. I met Megi Ibrahimi, a 20-year-old student at the Polytechnic University of Tirana, in late October, not long after I arrived in the capital. She told me that she had been studying with friends in a café in May when she saw a video filling social media across Albania. Razor-wire fencing had gone up around an idyllic strip of beach between the Adriatic Sea and a lagoon. The area had been a legally protected landscape since 2004. Loggerhead turtles lay eggs in the dunes. Mediterranean monk seals, some of the world’s rarest mammals, hunt in the waters. But in February 2024, Albania’s Parliament, in Rama’s grip, passed a law allowing resorts of five stars or more to be built in nature sanctuaries. Three weeks later, Kushner posted renderings of his project on Instagram—a 657-acre resort with a yacht club, casino, and beachfront housing that a leaked project document calls “Billionaire Villas.” (The average annual salary in Albania is roughly $14,000.) Later that year, a government committee led by Rama gave Kushner and his partners “strategic investor” status to build another resort on a nearby island, qualifying them for fast-track permitting and state-sponsored perks, including a cleanup of unexploded ordnance. (The island was once a Soviet submarine base.) In the video on Ibrahimi’s phone, a protester at Kushner’s lagoon site—a fisherman with ancestral ties to the land—is beaten, then dragged away by the developers’ private security guards. The man later claimed that the guards put guns to his head. State police officers stood doing nothing, until protesters, galled by the abduction, were on the verge of a riot. To Ibrahimi, and to many other Albanians I spoke with, the episode was a metaphor for their own feelings of powerlessness. The country’s leaders lavish favors on foreign investors, oligarchs, and party hacks, while everyone else struggles to stand. Ibrahimi, the daughter of a teacher and a retired municipal worker, graduated second in her high-school class, in the small inland town of Përmet. She could easily join the emigrants seeking better schools and jobs abroad. But she wants to stay. “I’m Albanian, and I want to live in my country,” she said. Yet the video she watched at the café that day sickened her: “It felt like our dignity was being dragged through the dunes.” She wasn’t alone. The protests at the resort site spread overnight to the capital, two hours’ drive to the north. Demonstrators carried signs that said Albania is not for sale and held daily protests through the summer. At their peak, in mid-June, the crowds had grown to an estimated 100,000 people. Ibrahimi spent much of the summer among them. She made friends and Instagram videos. She worked with other students on creative displays that she hoped would energize her fellow citizens, including a poker table that students sat around wearing masks with the faces of Albanian politicians, wagering chips that represented the country’s wildlife preserves. Outrage toward Kushner’s project mushroomed into a broad set of anti-government grievances, including corruption, school conditions, and living costs. Ibrahimi reveled in a sense of possibility. With so many people protesting—mothers pushing strollers, children making paintings, pensioners sharing memories of the country’s repressive past—she believed that Rama would accede to at least some of their requests. The protests were shaping up to be the most significant civic movement in Albania since pro-democracy students had toppled the statue of the late dictator Enver Hoxha, and with it nearly five decades of communism , in 1991. But Rama has dug in. A charismatic former professional basketball player and an accomplished painter, he has been elected to four consecutive terms and has zealously marketed Albania to the outside world, seeking tourists and private investors. He has made admission to the European Union his government’s highest priority. “There is absolutely no chance that the investment will stop as long as I am here,” he told Reuters in early June. As summer ended and the days shortened, people with kids and careers started to attend the protests less often. Ibrahimi and her friends came to believe that the responsibility for change in Albania lay with their generation. Her grandparents had suffered through the worst years of communism, when dissent got people jailed or killed. Her parents worry about what could happen to her at the protests, where students have been maimed, surveilled, and arrested. “My mom begs me every day to stay home, to not go outside,” she said. “But we still have dreams, and the time to fight for our dreams.” The Flamingo protesters initially had five demands, including term limits for the prime minister and the repeal of laws that benefited Kushner’s projects. In the face of Rama’s intransigence, student activists narrowed their demands to one: Rama’s resignation. They set October 13, a week after school resumed, as the start of a new, student-led wave of demonstrations. They called on protesters to meet in a new location, the Ministry of Education, at a time when many classes let out. Ibrahimi spray-painted the date around Tirana and promoted it on a local TV show. “We will leave the public square,” she told her interviewer, “the moment the main demand of this protest is met, which has been there since day one: the removal of this outdated political caste.” By the end of October 13, Tirana had descended into chaos. Protesters in masks threw stones, fireworks, and petrol bombs at government buildings and the police. They tore down streetlights, snarling traffic, and used signposts to batter windows and doors. In the days that followed, they set fire to banks, government ministries, a police station, and the supreme court. Ibrahimi brought eggs and water balloons filled with paint. For a time, she was on the front lines, face-to-face with the police, some of whom shot protesters with rubber bullets. But she soon found a role that felt more useful. She put on her gas mask and looked for protesters who were struggling to breathe. She led them out of the clouds of tear gas and flushed their eyes with the saline solution she kept in bottles in her backpack. In my conversations with Albanian political analysts, officials from minority parties, and others, I heard little condemnation of the violence. “It was unavoidable,” Arlind Qori, a political scientist who chairs the Together Movement, a party with one seat in Parliament, said when we met in his office. A sticker on the table between us depicted Rama behind bars, with dollar and euro symbols in his eyes. “Peaceful protests didn’t move him a bit.” As of late October, 107 protesters and 201 state police officers had been injured, according to official figures. Protesters have demanded a new, transitional government, but Rama—who has nearly three years left in his term—has no plans to step down. Rama told me that “the whole outrage against the project has been a big bullshit”—driven, he claimed, by journalists’ animus toward Kushner and President Trump. “Yes, corruption has been a big problem for Albania, and it would be a lie to say they”—the protesters—“do not have a point.” But independent prosecutors were rooting it out, “including within our own ranks,” he said. He blamed the recent violence on antifa, organized crime, and his political foes. “The opposition wants me to leave through street pressure, because it cannot defeat me at the ballot box.” Kushner’s projects are under review and have received no final approvals. In a recent statement on his website , Kushner acknowledged that locals have “legitimate questions and concerns.” He added, “Ultimately, Albania will decide whether the project proceeds.” Students describe their movement as leaderless. They fear that anyone they choose as a representative will be corrupted by the ruling party—or singled out for attack. Just 2.8 percent of Albanians polled in 2018 agreed that “most people can be trusted,” the second-lowest of nearly 90 countries in an international survey and the lowest in Europe. Still, Ibrahimi and her friends closely watched the recent elections in nearby Serbia. There, a student-led opposition defeated the populist strongman Aleksandar Vučić, who, like Rama, had dominated the country’s institutions for more than a decade. Also like Rama, Vučić had championed a Kushner-backed luxury real-estate development in his country. Kushner abandoned it in 2025 , after Serbian prosecutors charged officials with corruption in connection with the project. “There are things we could learn from them,” Ibrahimi said of Serbia’s student movement. An hour after our first interview, I found her again, outside the education ministry. Protesters had set fire to a few dumpsters, but the crowd was small, and people seemed tired. Ibrahimi flitted among groups of friends, some of whom wondered whether the time had come for yet another shift in strategy. As smoke poured through the afternoon light, an old woman arrived, pushing a wire shopping cart. She pulled faded winter jackets from a plastic bag and held them up to see which of the young people they might fit. She told Ibrahimi’s friends that the jackets had belonged to her children, who now lived abroad. It was getting chilly. Her children, she said, would have wanted this new generation to have them. This article appears in the January 2027 print edition with the headline “The Albanians Have Had Enough.”

items.title: UGEL CEO threatened me with trespassing warning ahead of inspection – Rent Commissioner alleges
items.description: Acting Rent Commissioner, Frederick Opoku, has alleged that the Chief Executive Officer of the University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL), Yawo Nutifafa Agbesi, warned him against visiting the university’s hostels for an inspection, threatening that such a move would amount to trespassing. Speaking in an interview on JoyNews’ The Pulse on Wednesday, November 18, Mr Opoku said he had formally written to the UGEL CEO, informing him of his intention to visit the facilities and requesting that they conduct the inspection together. “I wrote to the CEO of UGEL that I would be coming and that he should join us to go and do the inspection together. That is the best thing that anybody can do. But what happened? He responded two days later, at 7 p.m., warning me and telling me that I shouldn’t come because they are not under my regulation, and for that matter, if I come, it amounts to trespassing,” he recounted. Mr Opoku said the response prompted him to insist on proceeding with the inspection. “So I also responded at 10 o’clock p.m. that I’m coming. So if he has balls, he should stop me. That is why I went there to prove to him that I am coming there and nothing can stop me.’ His comments come amid the disagreement between the Rent Control Department and UGEL over hostel rental charges at the University of Ghana. The exercise reportedly resulted in a heated exchange between the Rent commissioer and the hostel manager, nearly escalating into a physical altercation.

items.title: Nigerian Army is winning war against insurgency – COAS
items.description: The Chief of Army Staff, Lt Gen Waidi Shaibu, says the Nigerian Army is recording significant successes in the counter-insurgency operations across the country. Shaibu stated this at the maiden edition of the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps (NAAC) Biennial Conference, Reunion and Pulling Out Ceremony, on Wednesday in Bauchi. The theme of the conference is “Emerging Trends in Tank Warfare for Enhanced Counter Terrorism and Counter Insurgency Operations in Nigeria”. He said that the army was making significant progress in the counter-insurgency operations in all the geopolitical zones. “We are certainly on track and focused. The NAAC remains a key player in the fight against insurgency, banditry, kidnappings among other forms of insecurity challenges across the nation, with remarkable successes,” he said. Shaibu tasked the corps to sustain the good work in synergy with other corps and security agencies to defeat security challenges bedevilling the country. He said the biennial conference marked another milestone in ensuring that the Nigerian Army paid greater attention to the sharing of knowledge, especially from the fountain and pool of retired senior officers for its advancement. The army chief described the biennial conference as one of the several initiatives aimed at encouraging the NAAC to contribute its quota toward discussing critical issues affecting the NA and suggesting viable solutions. “This event comes at a time when our involvement in several operations across the country has brought to fore the need for ingenuity, adaptability and a long-term approach to deal with the security threats which have also evolved,’’ he said. “This Biennial Conference and Reunion is therefore designed to provide us with contemporary approaches to solve our operational challenges,” he said. According to Shaibu, the conference will focus on gaining insights from participants’ experiences to improve planning, training and conduct of operations against myriads of security concerns and evolving threats facing the country. He said that the outcomes of the conference would better inform the army towards strengthening its fighting power. While commending President Bola Tinubu for his support, Shaibu urged the NAAC and other corps to use this strategy to reform the conduct of reunion by drawing extensively from the pool of knowledge from retired officers for the benefit of the army. Maj.-Gen. UB Abubakar, the Commander, NAAC Bauchi, said that it was designed to provide a platform for operational engagement, systematic review of operational experience and strengthening leadership. He said that the inclusion of the reunion into the conference offered opportunities to reconnect, share experience and strengthen the esprit de corps. Gov. Bala Mohammed hailed the army personnel for their gallantry and sacrifices in ensuring peace and security in the country. Represented by his deputy, Auwal Jatau, the governor said investment in infrastructure, agriculture, education and social services are essential components of peace and security in the society. He said that the state government would continue to implement social security policies to reduce poverty and empower youth to strengthen peaceful coexistence. The governor commended President Bola Tinubu over the establishment of military barracks in Alkaleri and Tafawa Balewa and pledged continued support to security agencies. Highlights of the event featured the inauguration of a dining hall and an officers’ mess at the barrack by the COAS. (NAN) The post Nigerian Army is winning war against insurgency – COAS appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: La ministre déléguée aux Armées : l’aide à l’Ukraine n’est pas responsable des difficultés économiques des Français
items.description: Alice Rufo a rejete le 18 novembre sur RMC tout lien entre les difficultes de pouvoir d'achat des Francais et le soutien apporte a Kiev. La ministre deleguee aux Armees s'en est prise a Marine Le Pen, a laquelle elle reproche de vouloir mettre fin a l'aide a l'Ukraine en invoquant les preoccupations economiques de la population. Elle a notamment critique les positions de Marine Le Pen sur le financement de l'Ukraine, lui reprochant de changer de discours concernant le credit de 90 milliards d'euros destine a Kiev. Elle a aussi reconnu les difficultes de pouvoir d'achat des Francais, tout en affirmant qu'elles n'avaient aucun rapport avec l'aide a l'Ukraine. Selon Alice Rufo, etablir un tel lien releve du mensonge. Elle a ainsi accuse la responsable du Rassemblement national d'exploiter les inquietudes legitimes de la population a des fins politiques qui serviraient davantage les interets de la Russie que ceux de la France. La ministre a juge « gravissime » la perspective d'un arret de l'aide financiere. Une presence militaire francaise revelee par RFI Les declarations surviennent dans un contexte de polemique sur la presence de militaires francais en Ukraine. Le 16 novembre, Radio France internationale (RFI) a revele que des soldats francais y etaient deployes depuis au moins l'ete 2026, dans le cadre de la mission Volia, notamment pour former des militaires ukrainiens et participer a l'entretien de leurs equipements. Selon RFI, le Parlement n'avait pas ete informe de la mission. Interrogee sur le deploiement, Alice Rufo a de nouveau defendu la position de Paris. Elle a evoque sur RMC « quelques militaires, experts et ingenieurs de l'armement » effectuant des missions ponctuelles, loin de la ligne de front. « Ce ne sont pas des unites combattantes », a-t-elle assure, ajoutant que la France n'etait « pas en guerre contre la Russie ». Le 17 novembre, devant l'Assemblee nationale, la ministre avait deja soutenu que la presence ne constituait pas une participation directe au conflit « au sens de l'article 35 de la Constitution », une interpretation juridique avancee par le gouvernement apres les revelations. Moscou met en garde Paris contre les risques d'escalade Pour Moscou, la presence de militaires etrangers en Ukraine depasse le cadre d'un simple soutien a Kiev. Le 17 novembre, le ministre russe des Affaires etrangeres, Sergueï Lavrov, avait denonce une « participation directe a la guerre », indiquant que la Russie avait fait part de ses preoccupations aux pays concernes par les voies diplomatiques. La porte-parole de la diplomatie russe, Maria Zakharova, a rappele les avertissements de Moscou concernant les contingents militaires etrangers. Citant Vladimir Poutine, elle a souligne que ceux-ci pourraient etre consideres comme des cibles legitimes par l'armee russe. En France, les revelations de RFI ont aussi suscite des critiques. Le 17 novembre sur LCI, le secretaire national du Parti communiste francais, Fabien Roussel, avait condamne un nouveau pas dans « l'escalade militaire », mettant en garde contre le risque de voir des soldats francais devenir des cibles et d'entraîner la France dans le conflit. Jean-Luc Melenchon a de son cote reclame le retrait des militaires francais d'Ukraine. Malgre les avertissements, Alice Rufo a maintenu la ligne du gouvernement. Elle a juge « gravissime » la reprise par Jean-Luc Melenchon, sur X, des declarations de Sergueï Lavrov, reaffirmant que les militaires francais deployes en Ukraine ne participaient pas directement aux hostilites.

Le Sénégal présente un portefeuille de projets
items.description: Lors du Sommet ouest-africain sur l’investissement et l’intégration (Waiis 2026), qui s’est ouvert ce 17 novembre 2026 à Freetown, en Sierra Leone, le ministre auprès du ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Plan, chargé de l’Économie, du Plan et de la Coopération, Alé Nar Diop, a présenté plusieurs projets structurants. Ils portent sur l’énergie, le phosphate et le numérique. Freetown – Le Sommet ouest-africain sur l’investissement et l’intégration (Waiis 2026) s’est ouvert hier à Freetown. Pays invité d’honneur, le Sénégal a été représenté par le ministre auprès du ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Plan, chargé de l’Économie, du Plan et de la Coopération, Alé Nar Diop. Pour lui, il s’agit d’un rendez-vous essentiel pour le développement économique de la zone. Ainsi, a-t-il dit, le Sénégal participe au Waiis 2026 avec un portefeuille de projets aux enjeux régionaux, répond chacun à l’un des piliers de ce sommet. Ces projets sont axés sur la construction de centrales électriques et énergétiques, qui étendent les programmes de conversion du gaz en électricité et en produits industriels et qui ouvriront l’électricité sénégalaise au marché régional. Les projets du Sénégal portent également, selon Alé Nar Diop, sur la valorisation des phosphates grâce à une plateforme pétrochimique et agrochimique qui permettra de compléter les capacités des ports miniers de Bargny-Sendou et de Ndayane. « Il y a aussi le numérique, afin de favoriser l’extension de nos capacités d’hébergement et de protection des données. Sans oublier le déploiement de la fibre optique qui nous permettra d’étendre nos réseaux de fibre optique à nos voisins », a ajouté Alé Nar Diop. La particularité de ces projets, considère-t-il, n’est qu’aucun n’a été conçu à l’échelle nationale, mais à l’échelle régionale, « car nous savons qu’un marché de 458 millions [d’habitants] vaut plus qu’un marché national unique ». Poursuivant son intervention, M. Diop a souligné que l’heure est au renforcement des actions dans l’espace Cedeao. Car depuis des décennies, l’Afrique de l’Ouest est perçue comme une région en proie à de multiples crises et chocs, économiques, politiques, sécuritaires et climatiques. « Il nous appartient aujourd’hui de créer une dynamique de renaissance, celle d’une région reconnue pour sa capacité à mobiliser des capitaux de manière durable afin de mieux valoriser son potentiel », a appelé Alé Nar Diop. Il a noté que notre région fait preuve d’une remarquable résilience, avec une croissance économique de 4,8 % en 2025, soit une performance supérieure à la moyenne mondiale d’environ 3 % selon les prévisions du Fonds monétaire international (Fmi). « Avec 456 millions d’habitants en 2024, dont 60 % ont moins de 25 ans et la moitié moins de 18 ans, notre région est l’une des plus jeunes au monde. Cette jeunesse représente un atout majeur pour réussir notre transformation numérique et optimiser notre potentiel minier », a souligné Alé Nar Diop. Parlant des atouts de la convergence régionale, il a mis en avant l’exploitation commune du projet Gta par le Sénégal et la Mauritanie. « Avec l’exploitation commerciale [de ce gaz] et la production de nos premiers barils de pétrole, notre pays compte désormais parmi les pays producteurs de pétrole. Fidèles aux idéaux panafricains, nous nous engageons à ce que cette énergie soit produite au bénéfice du Sénégal et de toute notre région », a indiqué Alé Nar Diop. Il estime que le Sommet ouest-africain pour l’intégration et l’investissement, vise à promouvoir l’intégration régionale par le biais du commerce, de l’énergie, de l’industrialisation, des stratégies minières, du développement des entreprises et de la transformation numérique. Cette réunion, à ses yeux, revêt une importance particulière. Car il s’agit de la première édition d’un sommet économique régional axé sur l’accélération des projets d’investissement fondamental et l’intégration commerciale de l’Afrique de l’Ouest. De notre envoyé spécial en Sierra Leone Demba DIENG

items.title: BoG reviews Women’s Development Bank application after receiving additional information
items.description: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) is reviewing an application for the establishment of the proposed Women’s Development Bank, following the submission of additional information requested from the promoters. Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr Johnson Asiama, says the application has gone through an initial assessment, with the central bank now reviewing supplementary information provided by the applicants. Speaking at the 133rd Monetary Policy Committee press briefing, Dr Asiama said the proposed bank forms part of efforts to liberalise the financial services space and expand access to financial services. “So far, the application came in. We reviewed it. We asked for some additional information. That information has been brought back in. We are reviewing it,” he said. The Governor expressed optimism that the review process would be completed soon to allow the Bank to proceed to the next stage of the application. “We are hopeful that very soon we’ll be through that stage so that we take it forward,” Dr Asiama said. The proposed Women’s Development Bank is expected to focus on improving access to financing for women, particularly entrepreneurs and businesses that face challenges accessing credit from traditional financial institutions. The Governor indicated that the Bank’s Head of Banking Supervision was available to provide further details on the application and the regulatory process. The development comes as the Bank of Ghana continues efforts to broaden the financial services sector and improve access to financing for underserved segments of the economy.

items.title: Una investigación independiente concluye que la actividad de Núcleo Nacional servía a los intereses de Rusia
items.description: Una investigación independiente ha constatado la existencia de conexiones en 11 países europeos del grupo neonazi Núcleo Nacional (NN), 14 de cuyos dirigentes fueron detenidos el pasado 6 de noviembre, acusados de los delitos de incitación al odio, asociación ilegal y tenencia ilícita de armas. Seis días después, el Juzgado de Instrucción número 1 de Gijón ordenó suspender sus actividades y congelar sus cuentas. Un informe realizado por Golden Owl, una startup vinculada al Parque Científico de la Universidad de Alicante y especializada en el análisis de inteligencia de fuentes abiertas, concluye que, aunque el grupo neonazi no tenía una posición oficial sobre la guerra de Ucrania y varios de sus miembros acudieron el pasado verano al país invadido por Rusia para recibir instrucción militar, en su seno operaba un sector favorable al Kremlin, que era el gran beneficiado de su actividad política. Núcleo Nacional ha confirmado este miércoles el fallecimiento en Valladolid de Enrique Lemus, de 63 años, fundador y jefe del brazo político del grupo, quien sufrió un infarto el pasado viernes cuando salía del juzgado. items.title: Advans Ghana Savings and Loans and Trans-Sahara Industries partner to finance electric motorcycles for commercial riders in Ghana
items.description: Advans Ghana Savings and Loans Ltd and Trans-Sahara Industries (TSI) have signed a partnership agreement to help commercial motorcycle riders in Ghana transition from petrol-powered motorcycles to electric motorcycles through hire-purchase financing. The collaboration brings together Advans’ asset-financing role and TSI’s electric-motorcycle assembly and deployment capabilities, giving riders a structured pathway to vehicle ownership while supporting more sustainable transport. The partnership forms part of Battery Electric Ecosystem Partners (BEEP), a multi-stakeholder network that connects financing, electric motorcycles, battery-swapping services, mobility platforms and rider training. By bringing these services together, the partners aim to address both the financing and day-to-day operational needs of commercial riders, commonly known as Okada riders. How the BEEP Collaboration Works Asset financing and a pathway to ownership: Advans, in partnership with TSI, aims to finance up to 10,000 commercial riders through structured hire-purchase arrangements. Riders will make payments over time and assume full ownership of their motorcycles once their financing obligations have been met. Income-generating mobility platform: Bolt serves as the mobility partner through which participating riders will work and earn income to support their vehicle-financing repayments. Electric motorcycles and local assembly: TSI has partnered with Tankvolt to introduce the TP 22 Plus electric motorcycle to the Ghanaian market. TSI’s assembly facility in North Industrial Area, Accra, supports its focus on local assembly, with plans to deepen localisation and develop the electric-vehicle supply chain. Battery-swapping and energy support: Kofa Energy serves as the ecosystem’s core energy partner, providing battery-swapping infrastructure and Battery Management Systems (BMS) intended to reduce charging downtime and keep riders on the road. Rider safety and professionalisation: The Commercial National Motorcycle Riders Union has endorsed the programme. Participating riders will receive technical, operational and safety training from Gear Shift Academy. Technical skills and servicing: Ghana TVET Services has partnered with TSI to provide training in the maintenance and servicing of Tankvolt electric motorcycles, supporting the development of a local technical workforce. Economic Benefits and Sustainable Mobility Asset financing gives riders a way to acquire an income-generating motorcycle through payments over time rather than paying the full purchase price upfront. The hire-purchase model provides a pathway to ownership, supporting riders as they build an asset for their livelihoods. Combined with electric motorcycles and accessible battery-swapping services, the initiative aims to reduce exposure to petrol costs, support more predictable operating expenses and improve operational efficiency. These intended benefits could help riders manage cash flow and strengthen household incomes; actual outcomes will depend on financing terms, operating costs and riders’ earnings. The transition from petrol-powered motorcycles to electric mobility is central to BEEP’s sustainable-transport ambitions. Alongside supporting adoption by commercial riders, the programme aims to stimulate local motorcycle assembly, encourage the development of an electric-vehicle component supply chain and create opportunities for technical training, servicing and skilled employment in Ghana. About Trans-Sahara Industries Trans-Sahara Industries (TSI) is a Ghanaian industrial and e-mobility company established to accelerate the transition of commercial motorcycle transport from petrol-powered motorcycles to more sustainable electric mobility solutions. Incorporated and operational since 8 September 2017 , . I i ts head office is at Tesano, Accra, and its motorcycle assembly facility is at North Industrial Area, Accra. TSI focuses on electric-motorcycle assembly and deployment, battery-swapping infrastructure and supporting technology platforms. Its integrated model combines electric motorcycles, accessible battery-swapping services and digital solutions to meet commercial riders’ operational needs. Through this approach, TSI aims to improve operational efficiency, reduce riders’ exposure to fuel costs, support more predictable operating expenses and contribute to sustainable urban transport in Ghana. About Advans Ghana Savings and Loans Ltd Advans Ghana Savings and Loans Ltd is licensed by the Bank of Ghana and is one of Ghana’s leading savings and loans companies, serving almost 160,000 clients through a nationwide network of branches and digital channels. Advans Ghana forms part of the Advans Group, an international network of financial institutions operating in six countries, with its head office in France, dedicated to expanding access to responsible financial services. In Ghana, Advans supports micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, individuals and local communities through financial and non-financial services designed to promote inclusion, enterprise growth and long-term development.

items.title: Los sindicatos UGT, CC OO y el ferroviario SCF firman la paz con Transportes en favor de reforzar la seguridad en las vías
items.description: El Ministerio de Transportes tiene ya en su mano un importante acuerdo con varias fuerzas sindicales ante la urgencia de devolver la confianza al sistema ferroviario y reforzar el mantenimiento de las infraestructuras y de los protocolos de operación. La compañía responsable del cuidado de las vías y de la gestión del tráfico, Adif, va a crear un grupo de trabajo con los representantes de los trabajadores para analizar nuevas necesidades en sus planes de mantenimiento de las redes convencional y de alta velocidad. También va a darse un vuelco al modelo de conservación de las infraestructuras con la promesa firmada anoche por altos representantes de Transportes y de la propia Adif de impulsar mecanismos para “reducir la externalización de la figura de los encargados de trabajo de las labores de mantenimiento, con el fin de incrementar la internalización”. Así consta en el texto de un pacto sellado anoche, cuando estaba a punto de concluir la jornada de huelga en el sistema ferroviario en favor de nuevas medidas de seguridad para la circulación. El texto no convence por ahora al sindicato de maquinistas Semaf, que mantiene la convocatoria de huelga para el próximo lunes. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Le Cheds mobilise leaders étudiants, acteurs sociaux et enseignants
items.description: Le Centre des hautes études de défense et de sécurité (Cheds) réunit, les 17 et 18 novembre 2026, des responsables d’amicales et des experts autour de la paix universitaire. Son directeur général, le général Jean Diémé, plaide pour des revendications sans violence. Faire des responsables d’amicales, des acteurs de prévention des crises et des partenaires du dialogue universitaire. C’est l’ambition du Centre des hautes études de défense et de sécurité (Cheds), à travers le séminaire national qu'il organise durant deux jours (17-18 novembre 2026) au titre du Programme jeunes, défense, sécurité et paix. La rencontre, placée sous le thème « Les présidents d’amicales et étudiants du Sénégal, leaders pour la paix et l’excellence universitaire », rassemble des représentants des étudiants et des experts sur la stabilité des campus. Pour le directeur général du Chefs, le général Jean Diémé, cette initiative répond à la nécessité d’aborder la sécurité sous un angle plus large que celui des seules questions militaires. Les tensions sur les campus posent aussi des problèmes de dialogue et de confiance. Le centre veut ainsi nourrir la réflexion publique sur la prévention des conflits. Le général Jean Diémé ne remet pas en cause le droit des étudiants à revendiquer. Il reconnaît aux amicales une mission légitime de défense des intérêts de leurs camarades. Il invite toutefois leurs responsables à privilégier la concertation et la recherche de solutions plutôt que le recours à la « casse ». Pour lui, le choix des présidents d’amicale comme principaux destinataires de cette formation tient à leur place dans la vie des établissements. Porte-paroles des étudiants, ils relaient les préoccupations sociales et pédagogiques, mobilisent leurs camarades et échangent avec les autorités académiques. Pour son directeur général, le Cheds entend renforcer leurs capacités en matière de négociation, de médiation et de prévention des crises. Les échanges doivent confronter les expériences et éclairer les tensions. Les participants sont notamment appelés à approfondir leur connaissance de l’histoire des mouvements étudiants, des textes régissant les universités, des libertés académiques et des franchises universitaires. Cette démarche a reçu l’appui du ministère de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation. Son secrétaire général, Fary Sèye, venu présider la rencontre, a salué l’initiative du Cheds, qui doit, selon lui, « renforcer la paix dans nos universités » et développer « une culture du dialogue permanent entre étudiants et autorités universitaires ». Il souhaite que les étudiants puissent défendre leurs demandes de manière saine et que les administrations académiques y répondent sans laisser les différends dégénérer en affrontements. Fary Sèye a par ailleurs indiqué que le ministère travaille avec les autorités académiques à une levée des suspensions frappant certaines amicales d’étudiants. « On est en train de travailler à ce que toutes les amicales suspendues, les autorités académiques puissent lever les suspensions. Et c’est en très bonne voie », a-t-il déclaré, en évoquant notamment la situation de l’Ucad. Daouda DIOUF

items.title: La Audiencia de Barcelona confirma las medidas cautelares contra Jonathan Andic: prisión eludible bajo fianza, sin pasaporte y visitas al juzgado
items.description: La Audiencia de Barcelona ha confirmado el auto judicial que ordenó el ingreso en prisión (bajo fianza) e impuso medidas cautelares a Jonathan Andic como presunto responsable de la muerte de su padre, el fundador de Mango Isak Andic. El primogénito del empresario fue detenido y puesto a disposición judicial el pasado 19 de mayo. Tras declarar, la jueza acordó (como había solicitado la Fiscalía) su ingreso en prisión, pero el investigado abonó enseguida la fianza impuesta (de un millón de euros) y eludió el ingreso en prisión. La Sección Novena ha ratificado las medidas impuestas por la jueza de Martorell (Barcelona) que investiga el caso Andic: comparecencias semanales ante el juzgado, retirada del pasaporte y prohibición de salir de España. La Audiencia avala así el curso de la investigación de los Mossos d’Esquadra y de la jueza, aunque contiene un voto particular, discrepante, del presidente de la sección. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Pochettino vows to end City’s dominance in Manchester as he takes charge of United
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Mauricio Pochettino has vowed to restore Manchester United as the most successful football club in Manchester, insisting the city’s balance of power will change under his leadership. According to the BBC, the incoming United manager made the pledge after the United States beat Haiti 2-0 in his final match in charge. The result completed an 8-0 aggregate win in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final. When former Manchester City player DaMarcus Beasley told Pochettino that “Manchester is blue; it will always be blue”, the Argentine replied, “No way, you will see. Give me time, and that is going to change.” Pochettino is expected to begin his new role on Wednesday after agreeing to a two-and-a-half-year contract. He replaces Michael Carrick and is set to lead United for the first time against Liverpool on Sunday. The 54-year-old said the challenge at Old Trafford was one he was eager to take on, while acknowledging the club’s current situation. “We’re excited because the new challenge is big, but it’s the adrenaline that you want to feel,” he said. “We are going to have a different job, but we have the experience to deal with that. We need to add our common sense in the way that we are going to approach all the things. “We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase.” Pochettino leaves the United States after guiding them to the 2025 Gold Cup final and the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup. He said he was proud of what the team achieved and hoped it would continue to grow. “Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to,” he said. “I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy.” The post Pochettino vows to end City’s dominance in Manchester as he takes charge of United appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Souveraineté alimentaire : le Gabon veut bâtir un nouveau modèle agricole à l’horizon 2030
items.description: Modernisation des exploitations, transformation locale, accès au financement et développement des infrastructures rurales : à travers le Plan de transformation des systèmes alimentaires (PTSA) 2026-2030, le Gabon entend faire de l’agriculture et de l’agro-industrie des leviers de croissance économique, de création d’emplois et de réduction de sa dépendance alimentaire. Les membres du gouvernement lors du lancement de l’atelier, le 18 novembre 2026. © Communication du vice-président du gouvernement Le Gabon veut accélérer sa transformation agricole. C’est l’ambition affichée ce mercredi 18 novembre 2026, à Libreville, à l’occasion de l’ouverture de l’atelier national de concertation sur le Plan de transformation des systèmes alimentaires (PTSA) 2026-2030. Présidant les travaux au Palais des Congrès Omar Bongo Ondimba, le vice-président du gouvernement, Hermann Immongault, a appelé à une mobilisation collective pour faire de la souveraineté alimentaire une réalité économique et sociale. Pour les autorités gabonaises, l’enjeu dépasse désormais la seule question de la disponibilité des denrées alimentaires. Il s’agit de réduire progressivement la facture des importations, de renforcer les capacités de production nationale et de faire en sorte que les richesses générées par la chaîne agricole profitent davantage aux populations locales. « La souveraineté alimentaire n'est pas un sujet de plus », a rappelé Hermann Immongault, soulignant son importance pour l’indépendance économique et la stabilité du pays. Mais cette ambition suppose de lever plusieurs obstacles structurels. Le gouvernement entend notamment moderniser les exploitations agricoles, améliorer l’accès des producteurs au financement et au foncier, développer les infrastructures routières reliant les bassins de production aux marchés et encourager la transformation des matières premières sur le territoire national. Autant de chantiers susceptibles de modifier les perspectives économiques du secteur. En favorisant l’émergence d’unités de transformation agro-industrielle, le pays pourrait notamment créer de nouvelles opportunités pour les jeunes, les producteurs, les coopératives et les petites et moyennes entreprises. De la production à la commercialisation, en passant par le stockage et la transformation, c’est toute une chaîne de valeur qui est appelée à se structurer. Mieux répartir les opportunités économiques dans les provinces L’objectif est également de mieux répartir les opportunités économiques dans les provinces, en faisant des territoires ruraux de véritables pôles de production et de création d’emplois. Une orientation qui nécessite toutefois des investissements, des mécanismes de financement adaptés et une meilleure coordination entre les acteurs publics et privés. Avec le PTSA 2026-2030, le Gabon entend ainsi passer d'une agriculture encore insuffisamment valorisée à un modèle davantage productif et créateur de richesses. Reste désormais à traduire les orientations de cet atelier en projets concrets, mesurables et accessibles aux producteurs. Car la souveraineté alimentaire ne se mesurera pas uniquement aux ambitions affichées, mais à la capacité du pays à produire davantage, transformer localement et rendre les denrées alimentaires plus accessibles aux ménages gabonais. items.title: Algérie : les paiements en ligne bondissent de 63 % en 2026
items.description: Le gouvernement se penche sur le paiement électronique, qui peine à se généraliser en Algérie. Le dossier a été au menu de la réunion du gouvernement présidée ce mercredi 18 novembre par le Premier ministre Sifi Ghrieb. Paiement électronique en Algérie : une feuille de route en 3 axes au menu du gouvernement L'état d'avancement de la mise en œuvre de la feuille de route relative à la modernisation des moyens de paiement électronique a été examiné, indique un communiqué des services du Premier ministre. Cette feuille de route qui, précise-t-on, vise principalement à renforcer l'inclusion financière, à moderniser les systèmes bancaires et financiers publics, à réduire l’utilisation du cash et à renforcer le suivi des transactions à l’échelle nationale, s’articule sur trois axes. Il s'agit de l’adaptation du cadre réglementaire et de la conformité aux référentiels de sécurité, du développement de solutions de paiement électronique et de la digitalisation des flux de paiement, ainsi que du développement des moyens de paiement électronique par secteur, rappelle le gouvernement. Forte progression du paiement électronique en Algérie en 2026 Quelques chiffres de la progression du paiement électronique en Algérie ont été fournis. Ainsi, indique le communiqué, la mise en œuvre de cette feuille de route a permis une « progression notable » de l’adoption des moyens de paiement électronique au cours des neuf premiers mois de l’année 2026, par rapport à 2025. Pendant la même période, les paiements en ligne se sont élevés à 391 milliards DA (+63 %), les paiements sur terminaux de paiement électronique (TPE) à 133 milliards DA (+48 %) et le paiement mobile à 56,4 milliards DA, tandis que les retraits aux distributeurs automatiques de billets (DAB) ont reculé de 14 % à 3 777 milliards DA. Le gouvernement se penche sur la numérisation des statistiques sectorielles Les autres dossiers au menu de la réunion du gouvernement sont la numérisation des statistiques des ministères, le contrôle des marchandises au niveau des ports et aéroports et l’homologation des produits de construction. Le Gouvernement a entendu une communication sur les mesures prises pour appliquer les décisions émises par le président de la République Abdelmadjid Tebboune lors de la dernière réunion du Conseil des ministres, concernant notamment la mise en œuvre des mesures réglementaires et opérationnelles relatives à la numérisation des statistiques des secteurs ministériels, ainsi que le système de contrôle des marchandises dans les ports et les aéroports, lit-on dans le communiqué. Homologation des matériaux utilisés dans les travaux publics Une autre communication a été présentée concernant la finalisation du cadre réglementaire relatif à la définition des conditions et des modalités d'homologation des produits de construction, d’entretien et d’exploitation des travaux publics et des infrastructures de base. Le renforcement du cadre réglementaire « revêt une importance capitale », compte tenu de son impact sur la promotion de l’utilisation de produits fiables et de haute qualité dans la réalisation des travaux de construction, d’entretien et d’exploitation des différentes infrastructures, comme les routes, ports, aéroports et chemins de fer, explique-t-on. Il s’agit, ajoute le communiqué, de « garantir l'utilisation de produits conformes aux normes et spécifications techniques en vigueur, et d'assurer un contrôle rigoureux des produits de construction, ce qui permettra de protéger les usagers, garantir la durabilité et la solidité des infrastructures et renforcer le respect des normes environnementales, ainsi que préserver le marché national en évitant la commercialisation de produits de qualité frauduleuse, non conformes aux spécifications ou dangereux ». L’article Algérie : les paiements en ligne bondissent de 63 % en 2026 est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Enregistrement des naissances : le BUNEC et l’UNICEF lancent la grande campagne nationale
items.description: © DR Sans acte de naissance, un enfant reste invisible aux yeux de la loi. Pour changer cela, un camion multifonctionnel offert par l'UNICEF au BUNEC a quitté Yaoundé pour une grande caravane nationale jusqu'à Garoua, afin de rapprocher l'état civil des familles. Un enfant sans acte de naissance, c'est un avenir freiné avant même d'avoir commencé. Pas d'accès garanti aux examens scolaires, pas de protection juridique complète, pas de pleine citoyenneté. Ce constat, le Cameroun a décidé de le combattre sur le terrain, au plus près des communautés. Depuis le 16 novembre 2026, le camion multifonctionnel de sensibilisation et d'appui à l'enregistrement des naissances, offert par l'UNICEF Cameroun au Bureau national de l'état civil, a quitté Yaoundé pour une grande caravane nationale qui va traverser le pays du Sud au Nord. Première halte le lundi 16 novembre à Abong-Mbang, aux côtés des autorités administratives et traditionnelles, avant de sillonner Bertoua, Meiganga, Ngaoundéré, Ngong et Garoua. Dans chaque ville, des séances de sensibilisation et d'enregistrement permettront aux parents de régulariser la situation de leurs enfants. Pourquoi Garoua ? Parce que lors du grand challenge national de la campagne « My Name, My Identity, My Right », lancé par l'UNICEF avec le BUNEC et le MINDDEVEL auprès des 374 communes du Cameroun, la commune de Garoua II est devenue championne nationale de la citoyenneté. Le 30 novembre prochain, ce camion lui sera officiellement remis par le Directeur général du BUNEC pour rapprocher durablement l'état civil des familles. Un acte de naissance, ce n'est pas qu'un simple papier. C'est le premier cadeau d'amour d'un parent, la clé qui ouvre les portes de l'école, de la santé et de la pleine citoyenneté. Avec ce camion, l'état civil se rend directement auprès des communautés pour qu'aucun enfant ne grandisse sans identité. Cet article Enregistrement des naissances : le BUNEC et l'UNICEF lancent la grande campagne nationale est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Daily Insight for CEOs: Building a culture of integrity and ethical leadership
items.description: An organization’s values are tested most clearly when leaders face difficult decisions. Integrity is not demonstrated by what an organization says in its mission statement. It is demonstrated by how its people behave, how decisions are made and how leaders respond when ethical standards are challenged. The CEO sets the tone for ethical conduct. Employees observe what leaders tolerate, reward, question and correct. When senior executives demonstrate honesty, fairness, transparency and respect for established standards, these behaviours become more likely to shape the wider organizational culture. A culture of integrity requires more than a code of conduct. It needs clear ethical expectations, safe channels for reporting concerns, consistent consequences for misconduct and leaders who are prepared to make the right decisions even when those decisions are difficult or commercially inconvenient. Key Strategies: Lead by example: Demonstrate honesty, fairness and accountability in everyday leadership decisions. Establish clear ethical standards: Ensure that employees understand the organization’s values, code of conduct and expected behaviours. Encourage speaking up: Create trusted channels through which employees can raise concerns without fear of retaliation. Manage conflicts of interest: Establish transparent processes for declaring and addressing actual, potential or perceived conflicts. Apply standards consistently: Ensure that ethical breaches are investigated fairly and addressed regardless of an individual’s position. CEO Leadership Actions. Review the organization’s code of ethics and ensure that it reflects current business realities and regulatory expectations. Create opportunities for employees to raise concerns and provide feedback through confidential and trusted channels. Demonstrate visible accountability by addressing misconduct consistently, including at senior leadership level. Actionable Tip. At your next executive meeting, discuss one ethical dilemma that could arise in your business. Agree on the principles and decision-making standards that should guide the organization’s response. Why This Matters? Integrity builds trust, protects reputation and strengthens the organization’s licence to operate. An ethical culture also improves employee confidence, supports responsible growth and reduces the risk of misconduct that can undermine years of institutional progress. About the Author. Ernest De-Graft Egyir, CEO advisor, Thought Leader and Founding CEO of Chief Executives Network Ghana, convenes the Ghana CEO Summit and served on Ghana’s Economic Dialogue Planning Committee.

items.title: Generation Ghana targets 50,000 jobs for young people in five years
items.description: Generation Ghana is targeting 50,000 jobs for young people over the next five years as it expands efforts to equip graduates with digital skills and connect them to employment opportunities. The organisation says only one in 10 university graduates secures what it describes as dignified and fulfilling employment within the first year after graduation, a situation it hopes to address through its Ghana Remote Online Work (GROW) initiative. Country Programme Director of Generation Ghana, Dr Vandyck Lomotey, said the organisation was determined to improve the employment prospects of young people by equipping them with skills that match the demands of the job market. “Currently, as we speak now, it is only one person out of 10 graduates who will get a job that is dignified and fulfilling within the first year of graduating from the university. That is the narrative we would like to change,” he said. The GROW initiative, implemented in partnership with the Mastercard Foundation, has supported more than 2,500 young Ghanaians over the past three years. It offers intensive training programmes lasting between eight and 15 weeks in areas including digital marketing, data analysis, cloud computing, web development and digital customer support. Dr Lomotey said the initiative had recorded a 70 per cent employment placement rate within 90 days of graduation. He said Generation Ghana’s focus went beyond providing digital skills, with the ultimate objective being to connect participants to jobs that offer sustainable incomes. “Our obsession as Generation is that we would be able to place people into jobs, jobs that would pay them a living wage, a living wage that their families, the individuals involved, can depend on and transform their lives and the betterment of society,” he said. One of the initiative’s key delivery partners, the Meltwater Entrepreneurial School of Technology (MEST), says its collaboration with Generation Ghana has helped expand digital skills training and improve participants’ preparation for the workplace. Programme Director of MEST, Olufemi Adewumi, said the institution had contributed nearly 1,000 young people to the pool of digitally trained participants under the initiative. He said the partnership had also influenced MEST’s approach to soft skills development, arguing that such competencies should be nurtured throughout the training process rather than treated as a standalone lesson. “Soft skills, at the end of the day, are a culture. It’s behavioural. You can’t teach people behaviour. You have to model it. You have to practice it and imbibe it,” he said. MEST has also expanded its web development training to include machine learning, artificial intelligence and Python, as it seeks to prepare learners for emerging opportunities in the technology industry. Mr Adewumi said the institution would continue exploring new digital professions and employment opportunities emerging from advances in artificial intelligence. The partners believe the target of 50,000 jobs within five years is achievable, but acknowledge that reaching it will require sustained collaboration and efforts to address broader challenges within the employment ecosystem. Dr Lomotey said Generation Ghana would continue working with industry players and government to remove barriers preventing young people from accessing decent employment. “We are not only just training, but the systemic challenges that lie ahead of us, we are working together to remove those challenges,” he said. The initiative aims to make digital skills a pathway to meaningful employment, helping more young Ghanaians secure sustainable incomes and improve their livelihoods.

items.title: GRA Customs intercepts suspected smuggled goods worth GH¢1.8m at Tatale
items.description: The Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) has intercepted suspected smuggled goods worth more than GH¢1.8 million at Tatale in the Northern Region. The goods were stored in a heavily secured warehouse. The seizure followed an intelligence-led operation against suspected smuggling in the area. The items included thousands of bags of rice and sugar, along with a quantity of cooking oil. The find is part of the Customs Division’s push against smuggling and other activities that cut into revenue and weaken the enforcement of Ghana’s trade laws.
